bibliographic.venue: International Journal of Emerging Research in Engineering and Technology, Pearl Blue Research Group
bibliographic.citation_apa: Gamarra, N. A. G. (2026). Trustworthy AI in Financial Risk Management: Applications for SME Compliance, Consumer Protection, and Audit Readiness. methodology.technology_context: artificial intelligence, machine learning, NLP, deep learning applied to financial risk management, compliance, fraud detection, credit assessment; no conversational or LLM-specific systems described

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The article addresses trustworthy AI governance, compliance, and audit readiness in financial risk management for SMEs, but the provided text contains no evidence of conversational AI systems, chatbots, agents, or LLM-based architectures central to the review scope.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the paper strongly aligns with regulated-domain governance themes (fairness, transparency, accountability, audit, compliance, bias, explainability) in financial services, it does not address conversational governance or LLM-based conversational systems. NLP is mentioned only as a general ML technique in risk assessment literature, not as conversational AI governance.

appraisal.notes: Conceptual/normative paper on trustworthy AI principles in financial risk management. Provided excerpts do not describe empirical sampling, data collection, or systematic review methodology; claims are largely principle-based with literature citations.

cerqual.explanation: The text coherently articulates trustworthy AI principles for financial risk and SME compliance, but methodological detail is unclear and relevance to conversational LLM governance is indirect at best.

coding.theme: Trustworthy AI governance in financial risk management
coding.subtheme: SME compliance, consumer protection, and audit preparedness

synthesis.main_claim: Financial institutions and SMEs need trustworthy AI frameworks—grounded in fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, security, and robustness—to manage risk, ensure regulatory compliance, protect consumers, and maintain audit readiness.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a principle-oriented account of trustworthy AI in financial risk management, including bias detection, model documentation, traceability, lifecycle management, and alignment with regulatory expectations for SMEs.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text does not specify empirical methods, sample, or evaluation outcomes; future work calls for more empirical studies. No conversational or LLM-specific governance mechanisms are addressed.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude as central or supporting evidence for conversational LLM governance; may serve only as distant contextual background on general AI governance in regulated finance if broader mapping is needed.
